These Black Friday streaming deals are some of the best we’ve seen yet, but make sure you read the fine print: Some are only open to new or returning subscribers, and others are for ad-supported plans, not ad-free ones. Still, they’re all worth checking out.
Also: Best early Black Friday deals
I’ve been reviewing streaming services for ZDNET and our sister site CNET for years, and these are my picks for the best Black Friday streaming deals so far that I’ll be tracking live through the holiday sale period — so you can finally join the conversation when your coworkers are discussing Widow’s Bay or The Gilded Age . Get them before they’re gone — they only come around once a year. We’ll continue to update this list as deals come and go.
Disney+ and Hulu’s best deal of the year is back, saving you $8 a month on the ad-supported plans for both streaming services for a whole year. (You can also get 31% off the Premium, ad-free plan, dropping it down to $14.99 a month from the usual $21.99 a month). After the 12 months is up, you’ll be charged full price, unless you cancel beforehand. But this is the best time to subscribe to these services, and watch everything from Toy Story 5 and Disney classics to The Kardashians and Dancing with the Stars.
Also: Disney+ and Hulu are 61% off for a year with this Black Friday deal – how to get it
HBO Max’s best deal of the year has finally arrived: New and returning subscribers can sign up now and get 50% off a Basic with Ads plan, dropping the price from $10.99 a month to $5.99 a month. This deal is offered as an add-on to your Prime Video account, or through HBO itself. After the year is up, you’ll be charged the current full price, but you can always cancel before if you’d like. If you’ve been considering subscribing to watch The Gilded Age , The Pitt , Hacks , or any of the tons of critically acclaimed original series and movies, this is the best time to do so.
Also: HBO Max is now 50% off for Black Friday – how to get the deal
Apple TV’s best deal of the year gives you six months of your subscription for $6.99 a month, down from the usual price of $14.99 a month. You can get this deal as an add-on to your Prime Video account to get the discount, or through Apple TV itself. You’ll have to cancel before the six months is up if you don’t want to get charged full price afterward, but that’s plenty of time to catch up on the streamer’s many award-winning shows, including Ted Lasso , Shrinking , Widow’s Bay , Severance , Slow Horses , The Morning Show , and Pluribus .

Though it’s only a deal for two months, getting Paramount+ Premium (with no ads) for $2.99 a month instead of the usual $13.99/month is still a great deal — and gives you enough time to watch the new season of Yellowjackets , or catch up with Landman or Dexter: Resurrection .

Our favorite Fire TV stick gets a big discount for Black Friday. “This streaming stick is really fast for the money, delivering snappier performance than my older Fire TV Sticks and even my Fire TV Series 4,” ZDNET smart home reviewer Maria Diaz said of the Fire TV stick. It supports 4K TVs, so you can stream 4K content without issues, as well as HDR10+, Dolby Vision, and Dolby Atmos, as long as your TV and audio system do.

This year, HBO Max’s Black Friday deal saves the most money. It drops the price of the HBO Max Basic with Ads plan from $10.99 a month (so $131.88 for the year if you pay monthly) down to $5.99 a month for 12 months (so that’s $71.88 for the year) — saving you $60.
If you don’t want to pay full price for these streaming services after the deal period is up, then yes, you can and should cancel. However, if you find yourself enjoying the service and willing to pay full price, you’re free to continue on and do so.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls as exuberance fades after Jensen Huang's return as CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls as exuberance fades after Jensen Huang's return as CEO
articles.content_orig:
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world  - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Trunmp and Xi ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen last week
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.
The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.
Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.
Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.
The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.
Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in Berlin in October
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.
He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared  to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.
If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

articles.title_orig: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.title_zh: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.title_orig: Op-ed: Trump’s Nvidia board intervention put a price on national security. Our adversaries will take note
articles.title_zh: Op-ed: Trump’s Nvidia board intervention put a price on national security. Our adversaries will take note
articles.content_orig:
President Donald J. Trump has accomplished something extraordinary. He directly inserted himself into the boardroom of one of America's most strategically important companies, Nvidia , helping to reverse a corporate leadership decision, and personally vouched for restored CEO Jensen Huang as having a clean bill of health regarding the national security investigations into his business activities with China.
On Monday, after Nvidia's board reinstated Huang following his resignation amid a counterintelligence controversy and allegations that Alice Huang, with whom he had an affair, is under suspicion of being a Chinese intelligence asset, Wall Street celebrated with a historic market bounce. But the market's enthusiasm should not obscure a far more consequential question circulating in Washington, D.C.: Does American national security have a price?
What happened at Nvidia raises the frightening possibility that it does, and it fits a recent pattern that is exactly what geopolitical rivals around the world want to see. Consider the economic pressures surrounding the Iran war. Disruptions to energy markets, shipping, supply chains, and consumer prices have complicated American strategic decision-making. These are notably different circumstances, but they raise the same troubling question about the costs of defending American national security interests, and when they become economically unpalatable to those in the Trump administration.
Beijing, Tehran, and Moscow are watching — as are our allies and partners — and they all may agree on one thing: America has an Achilles' heel that military and technological superiority cannot overcome. It is possible to impose sufficient economic pain to alter Washington's strategic calculation with friends and foes alike. Bleed American capital markets, disrupt commerce, squeeze consumers, and eventually Washington may look for an exit.
Despite the narrative that the president is weaving, there is a fundamental difference between responsibly weighing economic consequences and allowing adversaries to conclude that they can impose an economic veto over U.S. national security policy. Trump told CNBC in an extensive interview on Monday morning that when it comes to national security, "losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen ... would be a far bigger threat than anything we're talking about."
"The bigger impact was the long term. The bigger impact was you know he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said. "This was a big loss. This was a tremendous loss. And you saw that it affected the market. It affected even, I think it even affected the perception of our country in the world," the president said.
And that's true, but not only in the way Trump thinks it did.
This is not about whether Huang is a brilliant executive or whether Nvidia is enormously important to American competitiveness. Both are true. The question that America, particularly its government, must ask is whether Huang's economic importance justifies subordinating corporate governance, interfering with counterintelligence procedures, and stymying national security oversight.
Trump characterized the Justice Department's assessment as having exonerated Huang. Yet Nvidia's board reinstated him while its own review remained open.
The allegations involving reported contacts with Chinese intelligence assets do not establish legal wrongdoing. However, presidential personal assurances are not substitutes for independent counterintelligence assessments and investigations or congressional oversight. Monday's rising stock price might only measure what shareholders believe Huang at the helm of Nvidia is worth, while discounting or ignoring the unresolved counterintelligence risk that Huang may still pose to Nvidia and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem.
The Trump administration, Silicon Valley, and Wall Street may believe the matter is closed.
"That thing's like a rocket ship going in the wrong direction. Now it's a rocket ship going in the right direction, and it's taking the whole market," Trump told CNBC about Nvidia's 31.5% Monday gains.
One glaring vulnerability still on the horizon is what Washington does not know. If Beijing possesses additional damaging information, it controls whether, when, and how that information might be weaponized in an ongoing and now reignited strategic competition between the U.S. and China. Beijing retains the capacity to reopen this matter at a time of its choosing. Chinese intelligence could drip-feed disclosures, compel repeated explanations from Huang and the president, and transform Monday's declaration of resolution of this matter into a prolonged national security vulnerability.
There is also a striking irony here. Some pundits are comparing Trump's intervention to China's state-controlled market. To be sure, the Chinese government has a very heavy hand in its economy, but one thing the Chinese Communist Party will never do is put an individual ahead of national security and political authority despite the economic impact that this person or company is perceived to have. Xi Jinping and China's Communist Party have demonstrated a willingness to make almost the opposite calculation about national security and economic growth. Under Xi, national and political security generally takes precedence over the interests of individual companies and brilliant executives.
Consider Jack Ma. In 2020, Beijing halted Ant Group's planned $37 billion initial public offering and subsequently imposed sweeping regulatory restrictions on Ma's business empire. Beijing accepted substantial economic consequences to reinforce national security and political authority. This is not an argument for importing China's authoritarian model into American corporate governance. But the strategic asymmetry is noteworthy to revisit in this latest comparative context. Beijing has demonstrated that even its most celebrated entrepreneurs are not indispensable to the party and the nation. Washington risks signaling that some of its entrepreneurs are in fact indispensable to the state, which ironically potentially makes them even bigger intelligence targets for foreign adversaries.
As an economic matter, the commercial realities of Nvidia's China business make this situation even more perplexing. China, including Hong Kong, accounted for just 9.1% of Nvidia's reported global revenue in fiscal 2026, down from 19.2% the previous year. Its latest fourth-quarter guidance assumes no Chinese data center compute revenue. Nvidia did change the way it reports geographic sales, to customer headquarter address, in late 2025. But anyone familiar with Chinese strategic documents, including the 15th Five-Year Plan, should understand that Beijing has no intention of becoming permanently "addicted" to American chips. Its objective is technological self-reliance, not expanding Nvidia's market share and by extension its dependency on them.
Whatever the exact figure, I cannot think of a number that is worth selling out U.S. national security over, but it certainly isn't  9.1%, which is also a number that will continue to shrink. Furthermore, if the AI ecosystem is critical to our economy and our national security, then selling advanced chips to China or loosening export controls is the opposite of what we should be doing because the chips are used to juice the compute of Chinese LLMs that compete with ours, and to increase the effectiveness and lethality of Chinese weapons systems. The questionable sales of Nvidia chips in Asia, which are at the heart of this story, support neither our economy nor our national security. They undermine them both.

articles.title_zh: Beyond Jensen Huang, Nvidia and Alleged Spies: Court Records Reveal How Beijing Targets US Troops
articles.content_orig:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO yesterday , causing the company's stock to soar more than 30%. President Trump claimed credit for facilitating Huang's return . The CEO's comeback follows his resignation just two weeks earlier due to reports of extramarital affairs, including involvement with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, a close ally of the president, had previously donated $25 million to the new White House ballroom and security complex. His return boosted Nvidia's stock and triggered a rally in the entire stock market, revealing that one man's comeback is worth about a trillion dollars. Some individuals advocating for diversity and inclusion in Silicon Valley argue that Huang's return signals that profit is the only priority .
Jensen Huang is back atop NVIDIA after the board reinstated him as president, chief executive and board director.  "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in a statement. Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe hide caption
Ukraine recently sank a Russian warship in Libya , while Russian missiles struck Poland. There has been no comment from the Kremlin on the strikes. Depending on perspective, Russia's war in Ukraine appears to be either escalating or de-escalating. This month, the Trump administration said it is making progress towards a negotiated peace. However, fighting has expanded into Eastern and Northern Europe and the Mediterranean.
Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., has announced his resignation from Congress following a bipartisan investigation that found "substantial evidence" of his alleged sexual misconduct toward a House staffer . The House Ethics Committee determined that Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances" and disregarding the power imbalance in his relationship with staff. The report says his actions could amount to criminal sexual assault. Gomez, who has represented parts of Los Angeles since 2017, lost his reelection bid this fall to Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. Gomez says he has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.

Move over, violins and pianos. The Seattle Symphony is giving the timpani its moment in the spotlight with a world premiere concerto. Principal timpanist Eric Schweikert, who says he is drawn to the back-of-the-classroom vibe in the orchestra, is stepping up to showcase the versatility of the percussion instrument. The piece offers listeners a look at the timpani's range, including rumbling rolls produced with clever mallet work to imitate the effect of a long note. While Schweikert promises to deliver plenty of the wild, Muppets-style Animal energy audiences crave, he's also ready to keep his fellow musicians on their toes — and show the crowd that kettle drums can sing , too.

articles.title_orig: Venezuela moves toward possible debt restructuring with release of economic framework
articles.title_zh: Venezuela moves toward possible debt restructuring with release of economic framework
articles.content_orig:
Joseph Cotterill and Joe Daniels in London
Published November 24 2026
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Venezuela has unveiled debts of close to $240bn, as Delcy Rodríguez’s US-backed government published an economic framework for the biggest sovereign debt restructuring in history.
The South American nation’s finance ministry published up-to-date economic data for the first time in years on Tuesday, as the long-delayed anchor for what it said was a “clear and credible” plan to reduce the country’s debts and revive access to international markets following the US’s overthrow of president Nicolás Maduro in January.
Venezuela defaulted in 2017 after years of economic mismanagement, falling oil production and US sanctions that finally cut off payments and made a restructuring impossible for years.
Rodríguez’s government in May said it had hired a US adviser, Centerview Partners, to work on a restructuring, starting with an updated “macroeconomic framework” to guide talks. Venezuela is yet to release a full debt sustainability analysis on the scope for a restructuring.
Prices of bonds issued by the government and Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), the state oil company, rose about 2 cents to 3 cents on the dollar on Tuesday. The debts have gained about 70 per cent in price this year but trade at between a third and half of their face value.
Tuesday’s report said: “Venezuela’s public debt is in a state of protracted default and is unsustainable, reflecting the constraints imposed by financial sanctions, the decline in hydrocarbon revenues and years of macroeconomic imbalances.”
The FT in June reported the country was set to reveal a $240bn debt pile that was much larger than market estimates of less than $200bn. Tuesday’s report shows the difference largely consists of “non-financial” debts owed by PDVSA.
Preparations for a restructuring were delayed by the devastating earthquake that hit Caracas in June, people familiar with the matter said.
The figures released on Tuesday shine the most detailed light on the economy’s performance in the period since Maduro’s removal, which has included a US-backed investor rush for oil deals and the quake’s devastating impact.
The economy is set to grow 5 per cent this year, less than last year. Inflation is “exceptionally high” and is set to end 2026 at an annual rate of more than 300 per cent. It is forecast to fall to 72 per cent next year, according to the document.
Venezuela’s economy is seen doubling in size to $200bn by 2031 from less than $100bn just before Maduro’s ousting. This would be roughly half the size of the country’s peak GDP in 2012, in the last years of the rule of the late leader Hugo Chávez.
The small size of the economy and the resulting very high ratio of debt to GDP mean most bondholders expect to swallow a large reduction in the face value of their claims. However, they say the value of the restructured debt will depend almost entirely on how quickly the country can raise oil production and revenues.
Tuesday’s document forecasts PDVSA and international partners will spend about $160bn on oil projects over the next decade, with just under half coming from the state oil company.
Of a combined $237.5bn in debt owed by Venezuela and PDVSA at the end of last year, nearly half is made up of $110bn in defaulted bonds and years of unpaid interest.
The country also owes $6bn in bank loans and more than $26bn in arbitration awards — international legal claims that largely involve oil majors and miners whose assets were expropriated under Chávez.
China makes up nearly $17bn of $23bn in debt that Venezuela owes to official creditors, with $5bn owed to Russia. Just over $4bn is owed to multilateral creditors such as development banks.
The finance ministry said it had also identified $67bn in “non-financial obligations . . . entirely concentrated at the PDVSA level”, including $17bn owed to suppliers and $10bn related to joint ventures in oil projects. About $30bn of these debts are classed as “intra-public sector” obligations.
“These liabilities add an additional layer of complexity to the overall debt profile and underline the importance of a comprehensive approach when assessing the perimeter and dynamics of public sector indebtedness,” the report said.
Unusually for such a large restructuring, the IMF has not played its traditional role of leading the analysis of debt sustainability, despite Venezuela resuming ties with the fund this year.
Many investors and experts want the fund to be more involved. Some have questioned whether a deal on a debt workout is viable before elections, which US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said will “ideally” be held next year.
The Latin American Committee on Macroeconomic and Financial Issues, a regional group of independent economists, this month said Venezuela should hold elections and allow the IMF to conduct its own analysis before proceeding with any restructuring.

articles.title_orig: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'
articles.title_zh: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'
articles.content_orig:
The government has announced an independent inquiry into allegations rogue landlords in Birmingham are making huge profits by exploiting a housing scheme.
BBC Panorama reported last month that some companies in the city were taking advantage of the Supported Exempt Accommodation (SEA) system, intended to provide housing along with care and support for vulnerable people.
There have been claims of fraud, crime, poor housing and firms receiving housing benefits on behalf of residents but not giving them the support they are meant to.
A government spokesperson said an eight-week investigation would begin immediately, with initial findings and recommendations reported to ministers in the new year.
Sir David Pearson, chair of the Supported Housing Advisory Panel and social care expert, has been appointed to lead the investigation.
The government added the investigation would examine the scale of the problems in the city's SEA sector, including the quality of accommodation and support, use of public money, and effectiveness of oversight and regulation.
In a letter confirming the appointment, housing secretary Angela Rayner asked Pearson to lead a "rapid independent investigation" into the claims.
She said the investigation should focus on Birmingham, given consistent reports that the area was at the "epicentre of concerns" about poor-quality supported accommodation, while considering the extent to which any findings can be applied to the rest of the country.
"Good-quality supported housing can turn lives around and provide people with the support they need to live as independently as possible," Rayner wrote.
"There are increasing reports, however, that this system is being abused, with vulnerable people exploited at the expense of the taxpayer."
SEA is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse.
In many cases it works well for people, but BBC investigations over the past five years have uncovered stories of vulnerable people, including care leavers and people with mental health problems, being let down by the system designed to support them .
Some residents said they had been left living alongside drug dealers and criminals, and fearing for their lives, despite some providers reportedly claiming more than £200 a week at the time for every person they house.
Supported housing expenditure had risen faster in Birmingham than the national average in recent years, a government spokesperson said.
Pat McFadden, Work and Pensions Secretary, said there were "real concerns" about how the system was operating.
"Sir David's investigation will get to the bottom of what's going on, and where we find wrongdoing, we will act to make sure money is spent on supporting people who need it," he said.
The council paid out £404.4m for SEA in the 2024-25 financial year, with a further £211.8m paid between April and July 2026.
More than 34,000 people in the city currently live in SEA, compared to about 22,000 living in London, despite its population being more than seven times larger.
The BBC has previously heard evidence of claims that some housing providers were willing to make benefit claims for people who did not live in their properties .
The council introduced controls, requiring SEA providers to submit evidence they were delivering more than minimal care to their tenants.
But a recent internal audit showed the authority could not show the review had been completed for 72% of the claims tested.
At the time the results were published, 12,700 live cases were waiting review, of which around 7,100 had exceeded the six-month limit.
Bosses said a plan was in place to reduce the backlog to zero by the end of the year.
Preet Gill, the Labour MP for Birmingham Edgbaston, said she welcomed the independent review.
"I have campaigned on exempt accommodation for nearly a decade and worked with residents, the council and police to shut down Saif Lodge, the first exempt accommodation property in the country to be closed in 2021," she said.
"Neighbours have had enough of the antisocial behaviour, and vulnerable people are being let down while some providers profit."
It is not the first time politicians have investigated the issue.
An inquiry by the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee in 2022 reported that some vulnerable people had faced rape and exploitation by landlord "gangsters" in England's "complete mess" of an exempt housing system.
That was two years after Birmingham was named as one of five pilot projects designed to improve quality, enforcement, oversight and value for money in the sector.
Tuesday's announcement follows a recent letter to the prime minister from councillors Robert Alden and Ken Wood, demanding urgent intervention.
Campaigners have called for action for years, under both Conservative and Labour governments.
Alden, the councillor for Erdington and leader of the Birmingham Conservative group, said it was right that the government examines "why Birmingham has become the epicentre of this crisis and what must change".
"Residents deserve answers about how this was allowed to happen.
"Vulnerable people placed in badly run accommodation deserve proper support, and neighbourhoods suffering the consequences deserve action."
Charities, residents and politicians told Panorama last month that parts of the system were being exploited.
The programme found property agents drawing people into the taxpayer-funded system using social media videos offering free rooms, PlayStation consoles and holidays.
Patricia Coleman-Taylor, who runs Birmingham anti-poverty charity Narthex, said many vulnerable people were being used as "cash cows to generate income" that goes from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) into "the back pocket of the landlords".
Alysha told Panorama that she had moved into SEA 18 months ago, a survivor of domestic abuse.
She had nowhere to go and no family living nearby, so she was made homeless and relying on universal credit.
"I never thought I'd be homeless and I never thought my marriage would break down, but it did," she said.
"I felt extremely alone. I needed help getting myself back on to my feet, and that's how I got myself into supported accommodation."
She has since lived in three different SEA properties but admitted her experience was far from the fresh start she needed.
Alysha was forced to leave her first placement after just six months.
"There was one day at about 05:30 in the morning, where I was woken up to screaming and growling and banging.
"They'd been fighting really badly. The house was covered in blood, police were called, and the house was no longer safe."
Her second SEA initially looked "amazing" with brand new kitchen appliances and mattresses but Alysha quickly learnt it was not as it appeared.
Managed by a private provider, Alysha said she was promised weekly counselling sessions, access to food banks, and help with GPs.
"But it's not the case, it's not the case at all," she said.
"They're not interested, they come and they just want you to sign that paper to say Alysha's done support this week and that's it."
She added that the home had been left without heating at one point in the winter.
Jane and Melvin, residents living in Selly Oak, said the house next door to them was converted into SEA.
The couple admit at times they felt unsafe in their own home with the tenants of the property having involvement with guns, knives, and drugs.
"There were people overdosing," Jane recalled, adding: "Twice the front door was kicked in by people who didn't live there."
Jane said she and her husband never objected to the property being used to support people in need.
But she felt as though those living in the SEA were left to run "amuck".
"I think they were lacking the support that they needed, really," she explained.

The Iraqi government wants oilfields in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region owned by the federally-held North Oil Company to be placed under federal control after uncovering oil smuggling in the northern fields, Iraq’s Oil Minister, Basim Mohammed Khudair, has said.
“An investigation has been conducted, the findings of which will yield specific recommendations. There have been violations at oil fields belonging to the North Oil Company,” Khudair told Iraqi News Agency INA in an interview , referring to the uncovering of oil-smuggling operations.
The fields belonging to the North Oil Company “have been seized” by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), in addition to smuggling activities originating from other areas, the minister said.
The Iraqi Ministry of Oil believes that “the management of these fields should be federal, under the Ministry’s authority, consistent with how it manages fields in the central and southern regions,” Khudair told INA.
“The Prime Minister intends to resolve all outstanding issues and strengthen control over external border crossings by tasking the Iraqi Army with overseeing them, from the north to the south.”
The new showdown with the semi-autonomous region of Kurdistan is brewing just as Iraq is drafting and discussing its federal 2027 budget. Every year, the budget earmarks a share for the Kurdistan region.
For next year, the share for Kurdistan is kept at 12.5% of total spending in the budget.
But it also includes a provision that the KRG supply at least 400,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil to Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) for exports, according to the budget draft seen by Emirati news outlet The National . If KRG cannot export this volume, Kurdistan should deliver the crude to the federal ministry of oil for domestic use, per the budget draft.
Meanwhile, Iraq has boosted its crude oil exports via the Turkish Mediterranean port Ceyhan to 500,000 bpd, as OPEC’s second-largest producer has started trucking Basrah crude to the pipeline system to the north.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic shares tumble below $83 IPO price, on track to lose nearly $200 billion in value
articles.title_zh: Anthropic shares tumble below $83 IPO price, on track to lose nearly $200 billion in value
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic shares are back trading below the IPO price after a 13% sell-off Tuesday and a 1.5% drop Monday, despite a broad rally in most big-tech AI names. Trading below $76 Tuesday, the stock's now 8.5% below its IPO level and 34% below its intraday high of $115.
It took just four days for ANT to fall below its offering price, compared to 21 trading days for SpaceX, which rallied out of the gate.
Options volume on the stock is picking up as the shares drop and implied volatility jumps to 96, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Almost 500,000 options traded by noon E.T. Tuesday for a total premium of about $250 million, the sixth-most active single-stock options in the market, SpotGamma data show.
Almost 300,000 puts traded versus about 200,000 calls, but the sentiment implied by the trades was not overtly bearish, and judging by the biggest single trades of the day, traders are divided on what happens next.
The biggest single option trade of the day was a $7.5 million purchase of almost 11,000 75-strike puts expiring in mid-December. The trader paid above the ask, suggesting an eagerness to get the trade done at a cost of $6.85, according to SpotGamma. With Anthropic trading at $77, the position needs Anthropic to drop 11% by expiry to pay off.
"Anthropic remains bumpy as investors add risk to other names," said noted tech analyst Dan Ives.
Only one obvious call purchase appeared among the top 10 trades: a 3,000-lot purchase of 85-strike calls expiring Jan. 15 that cost $7.10 each, for a total of $2.2 million. That trade needs Anthropic to rally 19% within the next two months to break even.
Arguably the most interesting action was a string of almost a dozen put sales, ranging from $400,000 to $1.6 million each, all within moments of each other, selling the 120-strike puts expiring Dec. 18. The puts bring in $40 each, meaning the breakeven for the trade is at $80. Selling in-the-money puts in high-volatility stocks is often a way for traders to get long stock without the capital requirements of buying the underlying equity.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage, internal memos show
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage, internal memos show
articles.content_orig:
The risk of widespread technology outages could remain elevated in the coming months as organizations race to patch software vulnerabilities and upgrade aging infrastructure, Microsoft President and Vice Chair Brad Smith warned Sunday.
"I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks," Smith said on CBS News' Face the Nation . "The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now."
The warning follows a turbulent stretch of unrelated technical failures that disrupted major banks, airlines, air traffic control and Microsoft's own global cloud services. While officials have ruled out coordinated cyberattacks, the back-to-back disruptions underscored how heavily businesses, government agencies and travelers rely on interconnected digital systems.
Smith said artificial intelligence has accelerated the discovery of weaknesses in computer code. While that helps defenders fix flaws, malicious actors can use the same tools to target systems — forcing organizations to deploy updates at a breakneck pace that leaves less time for testing.
"What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you're a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems," he said.
Because organizations are patching vulnerabilities "at a pace we have never seen before," the rush itself creates instability, particularly on legacy systems, Smith said.
"Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you're trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can't take as much time to test what you're changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong," he added.
Smith urged consumers to install security updates promptly and called on companies to modernize older infrastructure and improve coordination with the government.
"If you get an update on your phone or your laptop with a patch, apply it because I think that's going to keep your technology far safer," he said.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered a similar assessment earlier on Face the Nation when he was asked by host Margaret Brennan about recent disruptions at major U.S. banks.
Bessent said Americans should not worry about the stability of their financial institutions, noting that banks have spent decades fortifying their cybersecurity and are "by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy."
Citing JPMorgan Chase , Bessent acknowledged that routine security patches can cause temporary glitches, comparing the process to routine medical care.
"I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine," he said. "Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency."
Still, some cybersecurity experts say traditional patching is no longer sufficient on its own. John Walsh, chief technology officer of IGEL, said in an emailed statement to Newsweek last week that operators of critical infrastructure must design systems capable of isolating failures before they cascade.
"For critical infrastructure, the objective must be to keep essential services functioning even when a component is compromised or unavailable," he said.
The recent wave of technical failures began November 12 and stretched into November 13, when a global Microsoft outage disrupted Microsoft 365, Exchange Online and Outlook email services for businesses and government agencies worldwide.
Smith said Sunday that Microsoft's outage was neither an AI failure nor a cyberattack, describing it instead as a "perfect storm" triggered by a software update from four months earlier interacting with a newer update and a shift in network traffic. Microsoft has published two reports on the incident and completed nine corrective steps, with 13 more planned, he said.
Also on November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration ( FAA ) issued a rare nationwide ground stop after a telecommunications failure disrupted its air traffic control network for roughly four hours starting in the afternoon, causing widespread flight delays and cancellations.
According to the FAA, its legacy network became unstable after receiving roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting communications and radar feeds across 17 of the agency's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. Investigators pointed to two possible sources of the surge, including an Arkansas communications site where defense contractor L3Harris was installing a router.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the shutdown to the age of the nation's air traffic control technology, saying overloaded switches and routers began producing inconsistent data.
Days later, United Airlines experienced a separate technology failure that disrupted departures across its U.S. network. Meanwhile, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase delayed transactions across parts of the U.S. banking system, and thousands of customers reported trouble accessing online accounts at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Capital One.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is "zero evidence" linking the incidents or suggesting they were the result of coordinated cyberattacks.
Smith said that while Microsoft's outage had other causes, many of the broader disruptions across the tech sector can be viewed as "AI ripple effects" stemming from the global rush to secure vulnerable code.

articles.title_orig: Trump shares meme of Jensen Huang raising red bra in air
articles.title_zh: Trump shares meme of Jensen Huang raising red bra in air
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang , two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.
The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.
After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International , a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.
"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook .
Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.
In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
Isabel  Vincent , Jennifer  Jacobs , Aimee  Picchi and Jo Ling  Kent contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration tees up tariff hikes on EU, China, others
articles.title_zh: Trump administration tees up tariff hikes on EU, China, others
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. trade representative's office is set to unveil its latest tariff plans Tuesday night.
The Trump administration will propose new tariff hikes Tuesday night on the European Union, China, Mexico, Japan and 12 other trading partners, a major step towards recreating the president’s global duties the Supreme Court struck down in February.
According to one person with knowledge of the planning, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will announce the new tariff proposals as part of a report into the countries’ excess manufacturing capacity. The findings are the product of a trade investigation Greer’s office launched in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the U.S. trade representative to impose tariffs in response to unfair trade practices.
Three other people briefed by the administration on the investigation confirmed the report was in the process of being finalized and the results would be announced as soon as today. They were granted anonymity to share details of policy plans that are not yet public.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the announcement was coming.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s intervention on Huang will exact ‘heavy cost’ on rule of law, national security: WSJ editorial board
articles.title_zh: Trump’s intervention on Huang will exact ‘heavy cost’ on rule of law, national security: WSJ editorial board
articles.content_orig:
His accounts continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, according to filings.
President Donald Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News.
His accounts have continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, including more than three dozen trades buying and selling millions of dollars of Nvidia stock this year through September, according to separate filings that disclose trades in his accounts.
The White House continues to maintain that third-party institutions manage Trump's accounts.
"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle.
"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."
Trump has repeatedly vouched for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid the scandal surrounding his alleged afair with a woman U.S. intelligence alleges is a Chinese asset.
On Monday, he took credit for Huang's stunning return to Nvidia , saying in an interview that he spoke "directly and indirectly" to the company's board members about bringing Huang back as CEO.
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump, who had urged Huang's reinstatement publicly, said in a phone interview with CNBC .
Following the announcement, the major stock indexes rebounded sharply on Monday as Nvidia shares closed up more than 30%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,447.98 points, or 3.0%, while the S & P 500 jumped over 4.73%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq soared over 6.5%.
Shares of Nvidia surged, recovering nearly all of the losses suffered since Nov. 12, the day Nvidia announced Huang's resignation .
Nvidia develops the semiconductor chips, systems, and software powering artificial intelligence. In early October 2026, its market valuation reached $5.8 trillion.
Given its significant presence in the stock market, Nvidia is a common holding in many investment portfolios and Trump's shares in the company represent a small portion of his overall portfolio.

articles.title_orig: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.title_zh: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.content_orig:
Late last month, CF40 Research , the research arm of the China Finance 40 Forum-a leading non-governmental think tank specializing in economics, shared its annual flagship report, China’s Economy: Toward a New Paradigm—Drivers, Trends, and Policy Implications , at its 2026 Bund Summit .
Guo Kai , President of CF40 Research and a former Chinese central bank official, kindly shared a copy and allowed me to share an excerpt.
The following passages are from the report’s English text. They have been rearranged and intervening material omitted; section headings and this introduction are mine. Corporate debt and profit figures below refer to its sample of A-share-listed companies outside finance and petroleum.
By 2026, the current real estate adjustment may not yet have fully run its course, but signs of structural stabilization have begun to emerge. After five years of deep adjustment, housing sales, investment, inventories, and developers’ balance sheets have entered a new phase, while house-price declines have begun to moderate. Few would expect the real estate sector to return to its former “golden age,” but the drag from the ongoing adjustment on the economy has diminished markedly at the margin. In other words, real estate is gradually shifting from the economy’s largest source of downward pressure toward a more stable influence.
Based on our analysis of international real estate corrections, China’s current real estate adjustment has already been considerable in both duration and magnitude, and the market has likely entered a bottoming phase. Further adjustment remains possible, but another sharp contraction appears unlikely.
Since the start of 2026, China’s real estate market has begun to show signs of “structural stabilization.” We selected 33 core cities for analysis, including the four first-tier cities—Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen—and major second-tier cities such as Hangzhou, Suzhou, Qingdao, Wuhan, and Hefei. We find that house prices, the floor area of new homes sold, and existing-home transaction volumes have all shown signs of stabilizing in these cities. House prices have even risen modestly in a few core cities. By contrast, real estate markets in most third- and fourth-tier cities remain weak. In other words, stabilization is concentrated in core cities rather than broad-based, which is why we refer to it as “structural stabilization.”
Thus, for the 33 core cities, if new starts continue to decline sharply, excess housing inventory could be rapidly reduced, potentially giving way to a shortage. This would provide additional support for house prices and demand and could accelerate the housing market’s recovery.
Over the past few years, the deep adjustment in the real estate market has been the main driver of the widening current account surplus. The underlying mechanism is that the real estate downturn led to a sharp decline in the investment rate, while the saving rate adjusted with a lag. The resulting widening of the saving–investment gap translated directly into a larger current account surplus.
As the real estate market gradually stabilizes, the drag from real estate investment will diminish, while household precautionary saving will stop rising. The saving–investment gap will therefore narrow, and the current account surplus will stabilize at a high level rather than continue to widen. This process bears some resemblance to the decline in China’s current account surplus after 2008, when the RMB 4 trillion stimulus package drove a sharp expansion in domestic investment, significantly narrowing the saving–investment gap.
By contrast, the stabilization of the manufacturing capacity cycle since 2024 has clearly not relied on comparable demand-side stimulus. Instead, the sequence has been “supply adjustment first, followed by a moderate recovery in demand”: a market-driven process in which firms voluntarily slowed investment and retired inefficient capacity in response to weak demand. This differs fundamentally from the post-2016 cyclical reversal driven by a sharp rebound in demand.
According to CF40 research, the new economy’s total value added rose from about 6.1% of GDP in 2018 to 10.4% in 2025, while the corresponding share for real estate fell from 12.7% to 8.4%. By 2025, the new economy’s total value-added share had surpassed that of real estate and had become an important component of GDP.
A defining characteristic of new-economy firms is their greater emphasis on R&D and their ability to generate more operating revenue and profits with less debt. In 2025, new-economy firms accounted for only 11.9% of the total interest-bearing debt of firms in the full sample, compared with 17.8% of total operating revenue and 29.5% of total net profits across the sample. Their share of total R&D expenditure was even higher, at 47.6%. As the new economy accounts for a growing share of China’s economy, the country’s growth model will gradually evolve.
The negative wealth effect of the real estate adjustment is fading, but households’ propensity to consume remains well below its pre-pandemic level, while further improvements in social security and public services are constrained by fiscal pressures. Rather than rising sharply, the consumption rate is therefore more likely to stabilize as the drag from real estate fades. If supportive policies are fully implemented, the consumption rate could gradually rise.
Moreover, the more advanced a manufacturing industry, the lower the share of output going to compensation of employees tends to be. For example, compensation of employees accounts for only 7.8% and 7.6% of gross output in electrical machinery and equipment manufacturing and automobile manufacturing, respectively—two industries that together encompass the “new three.” The corresponding share is 8.7% in computer, communications, and other electronic equipment manufacturing, the industry most closely associated with AI.
On a value-added basis, compensation of employees accounts for 36%, 42%, and 47% in these three industries, respectively, all below the service-sector average. This means that even if the new economy continues to expand rapidly and drive economic growth, households’ share of income in primary distribution will not automatically increase and could even decline. This is because these new-economy industries allocate a smaller share of their output to compensation of employees than the current economy-wide average.
On monetary policy, emphasis should move further away from pursuing credit-volume expansion toward lowering interest rates, improving inflation expectations, and restoring nominal demand. Real estate no longer performs its previous role in credit expansion, while the new economy is relatively less dependent on bank credit. Growth in bank lending and total social financing is therefore increasingly difficult to use on its own as a measure of whether monetary policy is sufficiently accommodative.
One possible aggregate benchmark is that “nominal growth in broad fiscal expenditure should exceed nominal GDP growth.” At present, local governments face multiple constraints, including declining land-related revenues, debt resolution efforts, and rising mandatory spending commitments. Near-term fiscal expansion will therefore need to rely more heavily on the central government.
The new economy has demonstrated China’s capacity to create new productive capacity, but the more important issue for the next stage is how to translate that capacity into household income and final consumption. New-economy firms have high R&D spending, high productivity, and low reliance on debt—an important direction for economic transformation. However, if the industrial structure merely shifts from traditional manufacturing toward more advanced manufacturing, higher productivity will not necessarily translate automatically into a larger household income share or a higher consumption rate.

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.content_orig:
At least 11 people have been wounded following a “terrorist attack” by Yemen’s Houthi group on a tower Riyadh’s financial district, according to Saudi authorities.
Those injured in Tuesday’s attack include two Saudi citizens, two Indian nationals, three Nepali nationals and four Egyptian nationals, a civil defence spokesperson said.
The Houthi group , which controls much of western Yemen including the capital Sanaa, has been firing at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen’s ⁠frozen civil war reignited in July in a knock-on from the US-Iran war.
Authorities said emergency services responded immediately and took the necessary measures to protect civilian lives and property.
In a statement, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthis said the “cowardly” attack targeted the King Abdullah Financial District, adding that authorities are conducting an on-site investigation.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense posted a picture of the landmark tower housing the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and the country’s tallest skyscraper. The image showed some damage to the building about halfway up the ‌facade.
Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi, Secretary-General of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), strongly condemned the “treacherous attack”.
“This attack is a heinous crime and an aggression that reveals the danger of this militia’s terrorist approach and its disregard for innocent lives, which requires a decisive international stance to hold this militia accountable,” AlBudaiwi said in a statement.
He added that the GCC member states stand with the Saudi Arabia and support it in all the measures and actions it takes to safeguard its sovereignty and protect its territory, citizens and residents.
The strike marks the second attack on Riyadh’s financial district in less than a week. An earlier attack on Riyadh caused “material damage”.
The Saudi-led coalition has not named the building that was struck on Tuesday. However, three separate witnesses said a strike targeted the PIF skyscraper.
A fourth witness told the AFP news agency that a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover.
No warning was sent to phones about any threats to the capital, as has been the case during recent strikes.
The attacks have caused ⁠the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh, ⁠and forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including soccer’s AFC Asian Cup. On the ground in Yemen, the war has caused a major humanitarian crisis, with ‌hundreds of thousands of people displaced from their homes since July.
The Houthis have seized swathes of territory, forcing forces aligned with the ‌Saudi-backed, ‌internationally recognised government to stage a major retreat this month. The Saudi-led coalition has conducted widespread air strikes.
